title: Mona Lisa Smile
full_review:
Domesticity gets a black eye in director Mike Newell's relentlessly grating melodrama, "Mona Lisa Smile" (Columbia), about a free-spirited academic who emboldens her female students to cast off the yoke of traditional gender roles. Ideologically lopsided, the film trots out the same hoary canards against marriage and maternity as roadblocks to success and self-realization and presents a skewed picture of nuptial life that borders on parody.

At the center of this paean to girl power is Katherine Watson (Julia Roberts), a bohemian proto-feminist from Berkeley who lands a post teaching art history at a conservative Massachusetts women's college in 1953. The propaganda-as-plot narrative follows a standard, free-thinking-fish-out-of-water formula.

First there is resistance, if not outright hostility, to Katherine's unorthodox teaching methods from the stodgy board of trustees and silver-spoon students. Of course, the girls' New England frigidity is soon thawed by the warmth of their new instructor's so-called liberating idealism. By the end of the film, the chintz curtains are cast aside by the winds of change and Katherine moves on to spread her be-all-you-can-be gospel, inspiring other women to shed the shackles of domesticity and enter the promised land flowing with careers and contraceptives.

Among the prim minds ripe for molding are Joan (Julia Stiles), an academic all-star torn between law school and her Ivy League boyfriend; Giselle (Maggie Gyllenhaall), the libidinous varsity vixen; and Betty (Kirsten Dunst), the snooty socialite who starts out critical of Katherine but winds up a believer. Along the way, Katherine locks horns with the college's by-the-syllabus president (Marian Seldes), befriends the spinster elocution and poise teacher (played by the ever chameleon-like Marcia Gay Harden), champions a martyred lesbian faculty member fired for distributing birth-control devices on campus, and falls for the lothario Italian professor (Dominic West). The fine talents assembled never really inhabit their roles, resulting in performances less about creating characters than serving as voices for the filmmaker's point of view.

The film's oversold thesis advances a toxic strain of feminism, which, rather than encouraging a deeper respect for the dignity of women, extols sexual liberation as an inalienable right, while painting marriage and motherhood as slave-state stumbling blocks on the yellow brick road to personal fulfillment. Married women are by and large caricatured as hypocritical gorgons like Betty's mother (Donna Mitchell) or prissy Stepford debutantes chomping at the bit to trade in their brains for a washer-dryer combo.

And while women, admittedly, have rarely enjoyed parity with men in our male-dominated society, the film's grievances against educational and social inequalities are poorly served by such heavy-handed stereotyping -- a cheap proselytizing tactic more suitable for the soapbox than the screen. In truth, the ideological girdle imposed on her students is much more constrictive than the corsets from which Katherine strives to liberate them.

Unlike Robin Williams' similar turn as motivating mentor in "Dead Poets Society," Roberts' efforts are not undertaken to inspire or expand young minds but only to tailor them according to her own narrow measurements. And while homemaking is paid lip service in the form of a Stiles tongue-lashing, the filmmaker's sympathies tip the ideological scale overwhelmingly in favor of those opposed to it as a valid life choice.

Apparently, Newell fails to see the irony in Katherine's demand that her linguistic lover stop his personal "tutorials" with his cooing students, after spending much of the film thumbing her nose at convention. Why should her personal moral dictates carry any more weight than those imposed by society? Like they say, people want morality to be subjective until they get their wallet -- or man -- stolen.

Nor does the film ever address what exactly Watson's -- and one assumes Newell's -- progressive philosophy is progressing toward -- a question commonly skirted by cultural relativists. You can only progress toward a fixed point. Once that point -- in this case, objective moral standards -- is deemed malleable, talk of "progress" is as futile and nonsensical as chasing the horizon.

Throughout the movie, art is used as an occasion to discuss deeper questions concerning conformity and self-determination. It borrows a pithy pearl from G.K. Chesterton: "Like morality, art consists of drawing the line somewhere." Unfortunately, this film asserts that art's purpose lies in erasing those lines. In the closing voiceover, the newly "liberated" Betty laments Katherine's departure but takes comfort in the knowledge that her teacher will "seek new walls to break down." There is one danger about knocking down walls: Without them, what will prevent society's roof from caving in?

Despite its breezy title, this "Mona Lisa" offers little to smile about.

Due to an antagonistic attitude toward traditional morality and an implied sexual encounter, as well as minimal crude language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
